newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Jospin pledges to curb 1998 budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jospin pledges to curb 1998 budget deficit.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Friday it would be difficult to manage the budget next year but pledged the public deficit would not be allowed to exceed three percent of gross domestic product.

In an endorsement of a Maastricht treaty requirement limiting budget deficits to three percent of GDP, he said France needed to meet this target not just to fulfil its commitments in Europe but also to prevent a rise in debt.
He also said France wanted a solid currency and that the recent rise in the dollar, while good for exports, also pushed up import prices.

In his first radio interview since taking office on June 3, Jospin said it would be harder to curb the deficit next year given the government will not have the benefit of the transfer of funds from France Telecom which filled a gap this year.
The transfer of 37.5 billion francs ($6.1 billion) from France Telecom to the state budget to cover pension liabilities reduced the deficit by 0.45 percentage points this year.

Even then, the deficit is running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of GDP, according to an audit of public finances released on Monday. The Socialist-led government has announced tax rises on companies to help bring this down by 0.4 percentage points.
It is now preparing a 1998 budget to be presented in September. "It is more difficult," Jospin said.

Economists believe France will seek to prove it can cut its deficit to three percent of GDP next year in order to assuage fears about any overshooting in this year's deficit beyond the 3.0 percent of GDP sought by Germany.
Jospin said he believed economic growth would improve next year, but declined to give a specific forecast. Higher growth would improve tax revenues, bringing down the deficit.

He also said he and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl both believed it was up to individual countries to take their own action to meet Maastrict criteria rather than worrying about what the others were doing.
He had been asked whether Germany was coming round to France's view that deficits should be reduced towards three percent of GDP this year and not necessarily to 3.0 percent.
"I would not say that Germany is coming round to France's view," adding that was not an expression he liked.
"I had Chancellor Kohl on the telephone yesterday and we discussed these issues. I think Chancellor Kohl approaches these questions in the same way as I do myself.
"Every country in Europe must do what it needs to do freely to meet the common goals," he said.

France and Germany have traditionally differed over their vision of monetary union, with Bonn insisting on a strict interpretation of Maastricht to underpin a strong euro and Paris arguing that priority must be given to jobs and growth.
Sketching out a path between those differences, Jospin said that Europe needed better growth and higher employment to ensure it had a solid curerncy.

"People are talking about the rise in the dollar at the moment. In some ways it is a good thing because it helps our exports but obviously every coin has a reverse side, in other words, when you import oil for example you pay more."
He noted that analysts had cited slow growth and high unemployment in Europe as a reason for the weakness in European currencies, particularly the mark.
"When the economy is not working, when there is unemployment, you pay for that on the monetary front.
"It is a useful lesson, and that is why we want to curb public finances, have a solid currency, while at the same time fighting against unemployment and weak growth," he said.
-- Myra MacDonald, Paris Newsroom +33 1 42 21 53 81 ($ = 6.179 French Francs)
